claim: Restriction of microvilli to the apical aspect of epithelial cells requires the localized activation of the membrane-F-actin linking protein ezrin.
source: Prior work has shown that restriction of microvilli to the apical aspect of epithelial cells requires the localized activation of the membrane-F-actin linking protein ezrin.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work in the field.

claim: Binding of PIP2 to ezrin induces a conformational change permitting the insertion of the LOK C-terminal domain to wedge apart the membrane and F-actin-binding domains of ezrin.
source: Binding of PIP2 to ezrin induces a conformational change permitting the insertion of the LOK C-terminal domain to wedge apart the membrane and F-actin-binding domains of ezrin.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including kinase assays and binding studies.

claim: The N-terminal LOK kinase domain can access a site 40 residues distal from the consensus sequence that collectively direct phosphorylation of the appropriate threonine residue.
source: The N-terminal LOK kinase domain can then access a site 40 residues distal from the consensus sequence that collectively direct phosphorylation of the appropriate threonine residue.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data using N-terminal truncations of ezrin-CTD.

claim: Ezrin is only phosphorylated at the plasma membrane with high specificity by the apically localized kinase LOK.
source: We suggest that this elaborate mechanism ensures that ezrin is only phosphorylated at the plasma membrane, and with high specificity by the apically localized kinase LOK.
evidence: This claim is speculative reasoning based on the experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: Ezrin is the founding member of the closely-related ezrin/radixin/moesin (ERM) protein family that serves as a regulated membrane-F-actin linking protein.
source: A critical component of epithelial microvilli is ezrin, the founding member of the closely-related ezrin/radixin/moesin (ERM) protein family, that serves as a regulated membrane-F-actin linking protein (Bretscher, 1983, 1989; Fehon et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Genetic knockout of ezrin in the mouse results in enterocytes with shorter and disorganized microvilli.
source: Genetic knockout of ezrin in the mouse results in enterocytes with shorter and disorganized microvilli.
evidence: This claim is supported by established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Loss of the single ERM protein in the fruit fly is lethal.
source: In the fruit fly, loss of the single ERM protein is lethal, but when selectively knocked out in photoreceptor cells, microvilli are lost (Karagiosis and Ready, 2004; Saotome et al., 2004; Speck et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: When the single ERM protein is selectively knocked out in photoreceptor cells of the fruit fly, microvilli are lost.
source: In the fruit fly, loss of the single ERM protein is lethal, but when selectively knocked out in photoreceptor cells, microvilli are lost (Karagiosis and Ready, 2004; Saotome et al., 2004; Speck et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: ERM proteins provide a critical function in polarized morphogenesis.
source: Thus, ERM proteins provide a critical function in polarized morphogenesis.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the genetic knockout data cited in the manuscript.

claim: ERM proteins are regulated by a reversible head-to-tail interaction.
source: ERM proteins are regulated by a reversible head-to-tail interaction (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by established scientific knowledge and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Ezrin contains an N-terminal FERM domain that binds the plasma membrane.
source: Like all ERMs, ezrin contains an N-terminal FERM domain that binds the plasma membrane and a C-terminal F-actin-binding domain (ezrin-CTD) that can attach to the underlying actin filaments that make up the core of microvilli (Gould et al., 1989; Turunen et al., 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Ezrin contains a C-terminal F-actin-binding domain (ezrin-CTD) that can attach to the underlying actin filaments that make up the core of microvilli.
source: Like all ERMs, ezrin contains an N-terminal FERM domain that binds the plasma membrane and a C-terminal F-actin-binding domain (ezrin-CTD) that can attach to the underlying actin filaments that make up the core of microvilli (Gould et al., 1989; Turunen et al., 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: In the closed inactive state of ezrin, the FERM domain is tightly associated with the ~80 residues of ezrin-CTD, masking the membrane association and F-actin-binding sites.
source: In the closed inactive state, the FERM domain is tightly associated with the ~80 residues of ezrin-CTD, masking the membrane association and F-actin-binding sites (Gary and Bretscher, 1995; Pearson et al., 2000; Reczek and Bretscher, 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The FERM domain and ezrin-CTD are linked by a ~150 residue α-helical region that folds into an anti-parallel coiled coil hairpin in the closed structure.
source: Linking these two regions is a ~150 residue α-helical region that folds into an anti-parallel coiled coil hairpin in the closed structure (Li et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior structural work.

claim: In the open structure of ezrin, the unmasked FERM domain binds the plasma membrane, the unmasked C-terminal domain binds F-actin, and the α-helical region presumably unravels.
source: In the open structure, the unmasked FERM domain binds the plasma membrane, the unmasked C-terminal domain binds F-actin, and the α-helical region presumably unravels.
evidence: This claim is partially speculative regarding the unraveling of the α-helical region.

claim: The unmasked FERM domain can bind many proteins, including the NHERF family adaptor proteins EBP50 and E3KARP, and the trans-membrane proteins CD44, ICAMs, and β-dystroglycan.
source: The unmasked FERM domain can bind many proteins, including the NHERF family adaptor proteins EBP50 and E3KARP, and the trans-membrane proteins CD44, ICAMs, and β-dystroglycan (Mori et al., 2008; Reczek et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: 10 nM LOK phosphorylates 18 µM ezrin-CTD.
source: In vitro kinase assay showing that 10 nM LOK phosphorylates 18 µM ezrin-CTD. Data are presented as mean ± SE, n = 3, two-way ANOVA (See also Figure 1—source data 1), ****p<0.0001.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: LOK phosphorylates full-length ezrin in the presence of 90 µM of PIP2 micelles.
source: In vitro kinase assay showing LOK-mediated phosphorylation of full-length ezrin in presence of 90 µM of PIP2 micelles. Data are presented as mean ± SE, n = 3, two-way ANOVA (See also Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and Figure 1—source data 1), ****p<0.0001.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: 18 µM ezrin is specifically primed by 90 µM of PIP2 micelles and not by IP3 or other phospholipids at 90 µM concentrations.
source: In vitro kinase assay showing that 18 µM ezrin is specifically primed by 90 µM of PIP2 micelles and not by IP3 or other phospholipids at 90 µM concentrations. Blots are derived from same membrane. Data are presented as mean ± SE, n = 3, two-way ANOVA (See also Figure 1—source data 1), ****p<0.0001.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Unilamellar liposomes DOPC:PIP2 (90 mol% DOPC, 10% PIP2) or DOPC:DOPS:PIP2 (80 mol% DOPC, 10 mol% DOPS, 10 mol% PIP2) promote phosphorylation of 18 µM ezrin by 10 nM LOK.
source: In vitro kinase assay showing that unilamellar liposomes DOPC:PIP2 (90 mol% DOPC, 10% PIP2) or DOPC:DOPS:PIP2 (80 mol% DOPC, 10 mol% DOPS, 10 mol% PIP2) promote phosphorylation of 18 µM ezrin by 10 nM LOK, whereas DOPC (100 mol% DOPC) or DOPC:DOPS (70 mol% DOPC, 30 mol% DOPS) fail to promote LOK-mediated ezrin phosphorylation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: DOPC (100 mol% DOPC) or DOPC:DOPS (70 mol% DOPC, 30 mol% DOPS) fail to promote LOK-mediated ezrin phosphorylation.
source: In vitro kinase assay showing that unilamellar liposomes DOPC:PIP2 (90 mol% DOPC, 10% PIP2) or DOPC:DOPS:PIP2 (80 mol% DOPC, 10 mol% DOPS, 10 mol% PIP2) promote phosphorylation of 18 µM ezrin by 10 nM LOK, whereas DOPC (100 mol% DOPC) or DOPC:DOPS (70 mol% DOPC, 30 mol% DOPS) fail to promote LOK-mediated ezrin phosphorylation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: 10 nM LOK-N phosphorylates 18 µM ezrin-CTD but not full-length ezrin in presence of 90 µM PIP2.
source: 10 nM LOK-N phosphorylates 18 µM ezrin-CTD but not full-length ezrin in presence of 90 µM PIP2. Data are presented as mean ± SE, n = 3, two-way ANOVA (See also Figure 1—source data 1), ***p<0.0002, ****p<0.0001.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F-G.

claim: The transition between closed and open ERMs requires phosphorylation of a specific threonine residue (T567 in ezrin; T564 in radixin and T558 in moesin).
source: The transition between closed and open ERMs requires phosphorylation of a specific threonine residue (T567 in ezrin; T564 in radixin and T558 in moesin) (Nakamura et al., 1995; Simons et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: In vivo phosphorylation of ezrin requires binding of the FERM domain to the plasma membrane phospholipid phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate (PIP2).
source: Additionally, in vivo phosphorylation was found to require binding of the FERM domain to the plasma membrane phospholipid phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate (PIP2) (Fievet et al., 2004; Hao et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: PIP2 binding to FERM directly changes the conformation so as to partially release the C-terminal domain to make the phosphorylation site accessible.
source: Structural analysis of the radixin FERM domain in the presence or absence of IP3 led to the suggestion that PIP2 binding to FERM directly changes the conformation so as to partially release the C-terminal domain to make the phosphorylation site accessible (Hamada et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior structural work and represents a hypothesis from that work.

claim: In the closed configuration of ezrin, the T567 that becomes phosphorylated is buried within the interface between the FERM and the ezrin-CTD.
source: Consistent with this model, in the closed configuration, the T567 that becomes phosphorylated is buried within the interface between the FERM and the ezrin-CTD (Li et al., 2007; Pearson et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior structural work.

claim: At steady state, about one half of the ezrin in an epithelial cell is phosphorylated.
source: At steady state, about one half of the ezrin in an epithelial cell is phosphorylated.
evidence: This claim is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: In vivo phosphorylation of ezrin turns over on the time-scale of minutes, similar to the lifetime of microvilli.
source: Moreover, in vivo phosphorylation of ezrin turns over on the time-scale of minutes, similar to the lifetime of microvilli.
evidence: This claim is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: A dynamic system of local ezrin activation by phosphorylation coupled with delocalized deactivation by dephosphorylation is a morphogenetic principle.
source: These observations strongly suggest a morphogenetic principle: a dynamic system of local ezrin activation by phosphorylation coupled with delocalized deactivation by dephosphorylation.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observations about ezrin phosphorylation dynamics.

claim: LOK and its close paralog Ste20-like-kinase (SLK) are the major ezrin kinases in epithelial cells.
source: Lymphocyte-oriented-kinase (LOK) and its close paralog Ste20-like-kinase (SLK) were then found to be the major ezrin kinases in epithelial cells.
evidence: This claim is stated as established knowledge from prior work.

claim: LOK and SLK are currently the only kinases known to selectively localize to the apical membrane of epithelial cells.
source: Remarkably, LOK and SLK are currently the only kinases known to selectively localize to the apical membrane of epithelial cells (Viswanatha et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: LOK was previously identified as the kinase that phosphorylates ezrin in lymphocytes.
source: LOK had previously been identified as the kinase that phosphorylates ezrin in lymphocytes (Belkina et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: LOK and SLK belong to the germinal center-like kinase (GCK) -V subfamily of kinases.
source: LOK and SLK belong to the germinal center-like kinase (GCK) -V subfamily of kinases.
evidence: This claim is stated as established knowledge.

claim: LOK and SLK consist of a conserved N-terminal kinase domain, a less conserved intermediate region, and a moderately conserved C-terminal domain.
source: They consist of a conserved N-terminal kinase domain, a less conserved intermediate region, and a moderately conserved C-terminal domain (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the domain structure shown in Figure 1A and represents established knowledge.

claim: A single ortholog of LOK/SLK exists in Drosophila melanogaster (Slik) and Caenorhabditis elegans (GCK4).
source: A single ortholog exists in Drosophila melanogaster (Slik) and Caenorhabditis elegans (GCK4).
evidence: This claim is stated as established knowledge.

claim: In Drosophila, Slik has been identified as the sole kinase that phosphorylates the single ERM ortholog, moesin.
source: In the fly, Slik has been identified as the sole kinase that phosphorylates the single ERM ortholog, moesin (Carreno et al., 2008; Hipfner et al., 2004; Kunda et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: LOK is highly selective for members of the ERM family, as the kinase's target sequences requires a conserved tyrosine at position −2 relative to the substrate threonine.
source: It is notable that LOK is highly selective for members of the ERM family, as the kinase's target sequences requires a conserved tyrosine at position −2 relative to the substrate threonine (Belkina et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: This is the first example of a protein that has to bind a phosphoinositide lipid to serve as a kinase substrate.
source: As far as we are aware, this is the first example of a protein that has to bind a phosphoinositide lipid to serve as a kinase substrate.
evidence: This claim is based on the authors' knowledge of the field.

claim: PIP2 binding to the ezrin FERM domain transmits a conformational change through the α-helical region to weaken the FERM/ezrin-CTD association.
source: Our results indicate that PIP2 binding to the ezrin FERM domain transmits a conformational change through the α-helical region to weaken the FERM/ezrin-CTD association.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental results presented in the manuscript.

claim: PIP2-priming of ezrin permits the LOK C-terminal domain to act as a wedge between the FERM and ezrin-CTD to allow the kinase domain to gain access and phosphorylate T567.
source: PIP2-priming of ezrin permits the LOK C-terminal domain to act as a wedge between the FERM and ezrin-CTD to allow the kinase domain to gain access and phosphorylate T567.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental results presented in the manuscript.

claim: A chimeric protein can recapitulate the activity of LOK in vitro and ex vivo.
source: In support of this model, we design a chimeric protein and show that it can recapitulate the activity of LOK in vitro and ex vivo.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: A distal site in ezrin about 40 residues from T567 is necessary for phosphorylation by the kinase domain.
source: Further, we define a distal site in ezrin about 40 residues from T567 that is also necessary for phosphorylation by the kinase domain.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data using truncated ezrin constructs.

claim: The LOK C-terminal domain negatively regulates the kinase activity of LOK.
source: In addition to being required for ezrin phosphorylation, the LOK C-terminal domain negatively regulates the kinase activity of LOK.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing inhibition by LOK-C.

claim: The PIP2-dependent mechanism of ezrin phosphorylation by LOK involves several distinct steps, thereby ensuring the specificity of the reaction.
source: Thus, the PIP2-dependent mechanism of ezrin phosphorylation by LOK involves several distinct steps, thereby ensuring the specificity of the reaction.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental results presented in the manuscript.

claim: LOK failed to phosphorylate full-length ezrin in the absence of PIP2.
source: LOK phosphorylated the ezrin-CTD as detected using pT567 antibody (Figure 1B), but failed to phosphorylate full-length ezrin (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: PIP2 did not influence phosphorylation of the ezrin-CTD by LOK.
source: In the presence of PIP2 micelles, LOK was readily able to phosphorylate ezrin (Figure 1C), but PIP2 did not influence phosphorylation of the ezrin-CTD by LOK (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The requirement for PIP2 in ezrin phosphorylation is specific, as other phosphoinositides, or soluble IP3, failed to substitute for PIP2.
source: The requirement for PIP2 was specific, as other phosphoinositides, or soluble IP3, failed to substitute for PIP2 in phosphorylation of ezrin (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The requirement of PIP2 for ezrin phosphorylation is not simply a negative charge effect.
source: The requirement of PIP2 for ezrin phosphorylation was not simply a negative charge effect as PIP2-dependency was reproduced in 100-nm-sized synthetic unilamellar liposomes of DOPC or DOPC:DOPS containing 10 mol% PIP2, which represent a more physiological system (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Both full-length LOK and LOK-N can phosphorylate ezrin-CTD, although the isolated kinase domain was less active.
source: In vitro, both full-length LOK and LOK-N can phosphorylate ezrin-CTD, although the isolated kinase domain was less active (Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: LOK-N was unable to phosphorylate ezrin, even in the presence of PIP2 micelles and unilamellar DOPC:DOPS liposomes containing 10 mol% PIP2.
source: Whereas intact LOK phosphorylated ezrin in a PIP2-dependent manner, LOK-N was unable to phosphorylate ezrin, even in the presence of PIP2 micelles and unilamellar DOPC:DOPS liposomes containing 10 mol% PIP2 (Figure 1G and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: In vitro phosphorylation of full-length ezrin requires both PIP2 and the C-terminal domain of LOK.
source: We conclude that in vitro phosphorylation of full-length ezrin requires both PIP2 and the C-terminal domain of LOK.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data presented.

claim: The FERM domain of ezrin is linked to the ezrin-CTD by a ~150 residue α-helical coiled coil hairpin, as represented in the structure of the close homolog Sfmoesin.
source: The FERM domain of ezrin is linked to the ezrin-CTD by a ~150 residue α-helical coiled coil hairpin, as represented in the structure of the close homolog Sfmoesin (Figure 2A) (Li et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior structural work and illustrated in Figure 2A.

claim: The α-helical region of ezrin consists of three α-helices that connect the FERM domain to the ezrin-CTD via an antiparallel coiled coil.
source: This region consists of three α-helices that connect the FERM domain to the ezrin-CTD via an antiparallel coiled coil (Li et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior structural work.

claim: In the absence of the α-helical region, the individual FERM and ezrin-CTD domains bind avidly together.
source: In the absence of the α-helical region, the individual FERM and ezrin-CTD domains bind avidly together (Pearson et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: A complex of isolated GST-ezrin-CTD and FERM could not be phosphorylated by LOK or LOK-N in the presence of PIP2.
source: Remarkably, while GST-ezrin-CTD was phosphorylated by LOK and LOK-N, we found that the isolated GST-ezrin-CTD+FERM complex could not be phosphorylated by LOK or LOK-N in the presence of PIP2 (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: LOK failed to phosphorylate GST-ezrin-CTD in complex with FERM in presence of DOPC:DOPS:PIP2 unilamellar liposomes.
source: Furthermore, LOK failed to phosphorylate GST-ezrin-CTD in complex with FERM in presence of DOPC:DOPS:PIP2 unilamellar liposomes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The central α-helical region is required for translating PIP2-binding to the FERM domain into a weakened association between FERM and ezrin-CTD domains, thus allowing in vitro phosphorylation of ezrin by LOK.
source: We conclude that the central α-helical region is required for translating PIP2-binding to the FERM domain into a weakened association between FERM and ezrin-CTD domains, thus allowing in vitro phosphorylation of ezrin by LOK.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data presented.

claim: Full-length LOK and LOK-N had about the same affinity for the ezrin-CTD (Km 252 and 176 µM, respectively).
source: Full-length LOK and just the kinase domain, LOK-N, had about the same affinity for the ezrin-CTD (Km 252 and 176 µM, respectively), but the maximal turnover rate for LOK-N was lower (kcat of 19.8 min−1 for LOK versus 1.4 min−1 for LOK-N).
evidence: This claim is supported by kinetic data presented in Table 1.

claim: The maximal turnover rate for LOK-N was lower than for LOK (kcat of 19.8 min−1 for LOK versus 1.4 min−1 for LOK-N).
source: Full-length LOK and just the kinase domain, LOK-N, had about the same affinity for the ezrin-CTD (Km 252 and 176 µM, respectively), but the maximal turnover rate for LOK-N was lower (kcat of 19.8 min−1 for LOK versus 1.4 min−1 for LOK-N).
evidence: This claim is supported by kinetic data presented in Table 1.

claim: In the presence of PIP2, LOK phosphorylated ezrin with a Km of 5 µM and displayed a lower maximal turnover (kcat of 8.5 min−1).
source: In the presence of PIP2, LOK phosphorylated ezrin with a Km of 5 µM and displayed a lower maximal turnover (kcat of 8.5 min−1).
evidence: This claim is supported by kinetic data presented in Table 1.

claim: In the absence of PIP2, LOK hardly phosphorylated ezrin, and the Km was of the order of 800 µM.
source: In the absence of PIP2, LOK hardly phosphorylated ezrin, and the Km was difficult to measure, but was of the order of 800 µM.
evidence: This claim is supported by kinetic data presented in Table 1.

claim: PIP2 enhances the affinity of LOK for ezrin by about 160 fold.
source: Thus, PIP2 enhances the affinity of LOK for ezrin by about 160 fold.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the kinetic data comparing Km values with and without PIP2.

claim: LOK-N phosphorylated intact ezrin so poorly that it was not possible to derive a Km value.
source: LOK-N phosphorylated intact ezrin so poorly that it was not possible to derive a Km value, emphasizing the importance of LOK C-terminal domain.
evidence: This claim is supported by kinetic data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The catalytic efficiency (kcat/Km) of LOK for ezrin and ezrin-CTD is 1.56 and 0.08 µM−1min−1, respectively.
source: Our data reveal that the catalytic efficiency (kcat/Km) of LOK for ezrin and ezrin-CTD is 1.56 and 0.08 µM−1min−1, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by kinetic data presented in Table 1.

claim: As a substrate for LOK, ezrin is about twenty-fold better than the ezrin-CTD.
source: Thus, as a substrate for LOK, ezrin is about twenty-fold better than the ezrin-CTD.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the catalytic efficiency data.

claim: The LOK C-terminal domain (LOK-C) must actively engage full-length ezrin in a PIP2-dependent manner.
source: Since the affinity of LOK for ezrin is greatly enhanced by PIP2, and this affinity is much higher than LOK for the ezrin-CTD, the LOK C-terminal domain (LOK-C) must actively engage full-length ezrin in a PIP2-dependent manner.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the kinetic data.

claim: LOK-C binds both the free FERM and ezrin-CTD domains with a Kd of about 10 µM and 2 µM, respectively.
source: Measurements revealed that the LOK-C binds both the free FERM and ezrin-CTD domains with a Kd of about 10 µM and 2 µM, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by binding data shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: Minimal binding of LOK-C to full-length ezrin could be detected in the absence and presence of PIP2.
source: We also attempted to measure the association of the LOK-C with full-length ezrin in the absence and presence of PIP2, but minimal binding could be detected (data not shown).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations.

claim: Priming of ezrin by PIP2 does not unmask binding sites sufficiently to enable the determination of a binding constant for LOK-C.
source: Thus, priming of ezrin by PIP2 does not unmask binding sites sufficiently to enable the determination of a binding constant.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the inability to measure binding.

claim: The C-terminal tail of EBP50 (EBP50t) binds to the same surface of the FERM domain that is occupied by a C-terminal α-helix belonging to ezrin-CTD.
source: Structural work has shown that the C-terminal tail of EBP50 (EBP50t) binds to the same surface of the FERM domain that is occupied by a C-terminal α-helix belonging to ezrin-CTD, thereby explaining why the binding site for EBP50t is masked in the full-length inactive protein (Finnerty et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior structural work.

claim: Both LOK-N-EBP50t and LOK can phosphorylate the ezrin-CTD.
source: As expected, both LOK-N-EBP50t and LOK could phosphorylate the ezrin-CTD.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Neither LOK nor LOK-N-EBP50t could phosphorylate full-length ezrin in the absence of PIP2.
source: When presented with full-length ezrin, neither kinase could phosphorylate ezrin in the absence of PIP2, while both LOK and LOK-N-EBP50t could phosphorylate ezrin robustly when PIP2 was included.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Both LOK and LOK-N-EBP50t could phosphorylate ezrin robustly when PIP2 was included.
source: When presented with full-length ezrin, neither kinase could phosphorylate ezrin in the absence of PIP2, while both LOK and LOK-N-EBP50t could phosphorylate ezrin robustly when PIP2 was included.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The chimeric protein LOK-N-EBP50t supports the PIP2-dependent wedge model by interaction of C-terminal EBP50t with ezrin FERM, compensating for LOK-C when ezrin is primed by PIP2.
source: Thus, the chimeric protein supports the PIP2-dependent wedge model, by interaction of C-terminal EBP50t with ezrin FERM, and consequently compensating for LOK-C, when ezrin is primed by PIP2.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data with the chimeric protein.

claim: Both LOK and LOK-N-EBP50t localized to microvilli in JEG-3 cells, whereas LOK-N did not.
source: Upon transient expression, both LOK and LOK-N-EBP50t localized to microvilli, whereas LOK-N did not (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Kinase suppression (sgLOK/siSLK) reduced ezrin T567 phosphorylation by over 80% and resulted in loss of microvilli in JEG-3 cells.
source: As with double siRNA knockdown (Viswanatha et al., 2012), kinase suppression reduced ezrin T567 phosphorylation by over 80% and resulted in loss of microvilli (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: Introduction of LOK or LOK-N-EBP50t into kinase-suppressed JEG-3 cells restored microvilli, whereas LOK-N failed to restore microvilli.
source: Introduction of LOK or LOK-N-EBP50t into these cells restored microvilli, whereas LOK-N failed to restore microvilli (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: LOK-N-EBP50t restored ezrin phosphorylation in kinase-suppressed cells.
source: LOK-N-EBP50t also restored ezrin phosphorylation in kinase-suppressed cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: LOK-N-EBP50t is able to recapitulate both the enzymatic properties of LOK as well as its function in microvilli formation.
source: Thus, LOK-N-EBP50t is able to recapitulate both the enzymatic properties of LOK as well as its function in microvilli formation, via restricting activated ezrin to the apical membrane (Figure 4E).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data with the chimeric protein.

claim: High expression of LOK-C in JEG-3 cells inhibits ezrin phosphorylation and results in the loss of microvilli.
source: High expression of LOK-C in JEG-3 cells inhibits ezrin phosphorylation and results in the loss of microvilli.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: In low-level expressing cells, LOK-C is localized to regions of individual microvilli with local loss of ezrin.
source: However, in low-level expressing cells, LOK-C is localized to regions of individual microvilli with local loss of ezrin (Viswanatha et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: LOK-C has the properties of a negative regulatory domain in cells.
source: Thus in cells, LOK-C has the properties of a negative regulatory domain.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the cellular observations.

claim: LOK-C inhibited the ability of LOK or LOK-N-EBP50t to phosphorylate ezrin with an IC50 of 1.9 ± 0.1 µM and 1.6 ± 0.1 µM, respectively.
source: In the presence of 90 µM PIP2, LOK-C inhibited the ability of LOK or LOK-N-EBP50t to phosphorylate ezrin with an IC50 of 1.9 ± 0.1 µM and 1.6 ± 0.1 µM, respectively (Figure 5A and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A and C.

claim: The inhibition curves with ezrin-CTD as substrate showed an IC50 for LOK of 1.9 ± 0.2 µM and for LOK-N of 1.2 ± 0.2 µM.
source: Similarly, the inhibition curves with ezrin-CTD as substrate showed an IC50 for LOK of 1.9 ± 0.2 µM and for LOK-N of 1.2 ± 0.2 µM (Figure 5B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B and C.

claim: Inhibition by LOK-C is due to a direct effect on the LOK kinase activity rather than affecting the substrate.
source: As these IC50 values were all much lower than the 18 µM substrate concentration, inhibition by LOK-C is due to a direct effect on the LOK kinase activity rather than affecting the substrate.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the IC50 values relative to substrate concentration.

claim: The similar IC50 values suggest that the mechanism of inhibition by LOK-C is similar in all cases, namely competitive inhibition.
source: These similar IC50 values also suggest that the mechanism of inhibition is similar in all cases, namely competitive inhibition.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the similar IC50 values.

claim: Binding of the kinase domain of full-length LOK to the ezrin-CTD likely relieves the inhibition imposed by its own C-terminal domain.
source: Moreover, since the IC50 values of LOK-C for LOK and LOK-N phosphorylation of the ezrin-CTD are similar, binding of the kinase domain of full-length LOK to the ezrin-CTD likely relieves the inhibition imposed by its own C-terminal domain.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the IC50 data.

claim: LOK has a strong preference for a tyrosine at P-2 (Y565), which is conserved in all ERM proteins.
source: In the case of LOK, there is a strong preference for a tyrosine at P-2 (Y565), which is conserved in all ERM proteins (Belkina et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Robust phosphorylation by LOK and LOK-N was seen up to GST-ezrin-520–585.
source: Robust phosphorylation was seen up to GST-ezrin-520–585.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: GST-ezrin-530–585 and GST-ezrin-555–585 were very poor substrates for LOK and LOK-N.
source: The shorter constructs, GST-ezrin-530–585 and GST-ezrin-555–585, were very poor substrates for LOK and LOK-N.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The region 520–530 of ezrin is important for recognition by LOK-N.
source: As this suggests that the region 520–530 is important for recognition by LOK-N, we made a construct, GST-ezrin-490-(∆520–530)−585, lacking this region.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the truncation data.

claim: GST-ezrin-490-(∆520–530)−585 was a significantly poorer substrate than GST-ezrin-490–585.
source: This truncated substrate was a significantly poorer substrate than GST-ezrin-490–585.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The ezrin-CTD has an additional distal docking site approximately 40 residues N-terminal to the kinase consensus sequence.
source: Thus, the ezrin-CTD has an additional distal docking site approximately 40 residues N-terminal to the kinase consensus sequence.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the truncation data.

claim: Specific morphogenetic components have to be controlled locally to maintain the morphological polarity of a cell.
source: In order to maintain the morphological polarity of a cell, specific morphogenetic components have to be controlled locally.
evidence: This is a general principle stated in the discussion.

claim: In the case of microvilli on epithelial cells, ezrin is locally activated through T567 phosphorylation mediated by the closely related LOK and SLK kinases.
source: In the case of microvilli on epithelial cells, ezrin is locally activated through T567 phosphorylation mediated by the closely related LOK and SLK kinases.
evidence: This claim summarizes findings from the manuscript and prior work.

claim: PIP2 is a regulatory lipid largely confined to the plasma membrane.
source: Since PIP2 is a regulatory lipid largely confined to the plasma membrane, the highly specific priming of ezrin by PIP2 ensures that ezrin phosphorylation is restricted to this membrane compartment.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge.

claim: The highly specific priming of ezrin by PIP2 ensures that ezrin phosphorylation is restricted to the plasma membrane compartment.
source: Since PIP2 is a regulatory lipid largely confined to the plasma membrane, the highly specific priming of ezrin by PIP2 ensures that ezrin phosphorylation is restricted to this membrane compartment.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental findings and knowledge about PIP2 localization.

claim: Both phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate (PIP2) micelles and PIP2-containing unilamellar liposomes prime ezrin for LOK-mediated phosphorylation.
source: Our in vitro studies show that both phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate (PIP2) micelles and PIP2-containing unilamellar liposomes prime ezrin for LOK-mediated phosphorylation, while other phospholipids and more importantly, IP3, the head group in direct physical contact with ezrin, fail to prime ezrin for phosphorylation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Other phospholipids and IP3 fail to prime ezrin for phosphorylation.
source: Our in vitro studies show that both phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate (PIP2) micelles and PIP2-containing unilamellar liposomes prime ezrin for LOK-mediated phosphorylation, while other phospholipids and more importantly, IP3, the head group in direct physical contact with ezrin, fail to prime ezrin for phosphorylation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Priming of ezrin for phosphorylation requires an appropriate charge distribution provided by phosphate groups in the head group of the phospholipid phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate, and a high local concentration of the head group that can only be achieved in vitro using micelles or liposomes.
source: From these data, we conclude that priming of ezrin for phosphorylation requires an appropriate charge distribution provided by phosphate groups in the head group of the phospholipid phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate, and a high local concentration of the head group that can only be achieved in vitro using micelles or liposomes.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data.

claim: PIP2 acts through ezrin activation, and not by LOK activation.
source: Therefore, we were surprised to find that in the presence of PIP2, LOK is unable to phosphorylate a complex of FERM associated with the ezrin-CTD. This revealed two points: First, PIP2 acts through ezrin activation, and not by LOK activation, and second, the central α-helical coiled coil hairpin connecting the FERM to the ezrin-CTD is necessary for priming of intact ezrin for phosphorylation.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data with FERM+ezrin-CTD complexes.

claim: The central α-helical coiled coil hairpin connecting the FERM to the ezrin-CTD is necessary for priming of intact ezrin for phosphorylation.
source: Therefore, we were surprised to find that in the presence of PIP2, LOK is unable to phosphorylate a complex of FERM associated with the ezrin-CTD. This revealed two points: First, PIP2 acts through ezrin activation, and not by LOK activation, and second, the central α-helical coiled coil hairpin connecting the FERM to the ezrin-CTD is necessary for priming of intact ezrin for phosphorylation.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data with FERM+ezrin-CTD complexes.

claim: The α-helical coiled coil region acts as a spring counteracting the strong association between the FERM and ezrin-CTD, and upon binding PIP2, the strength of the spring is enhanced.
source: The detailed function of the central coiled coil hairpin is unknown, but one attractive possibility is that the α-helical coiled coil region acts as a spring counteracting the strong association between the FERM and ezrin-CTD, and upon binding PIP2, the strength of the spring is enhanced.
evidence: This is a speculative model proposed by the authors.

claim: The proposed spring model has similarities in other proteins, such as the ERM-related protein merlin.
source: The proposed spring model has similarities in other proteins. In the ERM-related protein merlin, the central α-helical hairpin undergoes an unfolding event, like a 'switchblade', during opening of the protein (Li et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work on merlin.

claim: In the ERM-related protein merlin, the central α-helical hairpin undergoes an unfolding event, like a 'switchblade', during opening of the protein.
source: In the ERM-related protein merlin, the central α-helical hairpin undergoes an unfolding event, like a 'switchblade', during opening of the protein (Li et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The influenza virus hemagglutinin protein has a rod-shaped α-helical ectodomain that undergoes a dramatic 'switchblade-like' unfolding event at low pH.
source: Another example occurs within the influenza virus hemagglutinin protein. This protein is a membrane-fusion glycoprotein with a rod-shaped α-helical ectodomain that undergoes a dramatic 'switchblade-like' unfolding event at low pH (Skehel and Wiley, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The isolated LOK kinase domain cannot phosphorylate ezrin under any condition.
source: The active involvement of LOK-C (Figure 6B, step 2) is shown by the finding that the isolated LOK kinase domain cannot phosphorylate ezrin under any condition, whereas it can phosphorylate the isolated ezrin-CTD.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: In the presence of PIP2, the Km of full-length LOK for ezrin is about 45 times lower than for the ezrin-CTD.
source: Moreover, in the presence of PIP2, the Km of full-length LOK for ezrin is about 45 times lower than for the ezrin-CTD, indicating that the combined action of PIP2 and the FERM domain greatly enhances specificity.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the kinetic data in Table 1.

claim: The combined action of PIP2 and the FERM domain greatly enhances specificity of LOK for ezrin.
source: Moreover, in the presence of PIP2, the Km of full-length LOK for ezrin is about 45 times lower than for the ezrin-CTD, indicating that the combined action of PIP2 and the FERM domain greatly enhances specificity.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the kinetic data.

claim: LOK-C can bind with low affinity to both the isolated FERM and ezrin-CTD.
source: Consistent with the kinetics of PIP2-primed full-length ezrin, we found that LOK-C can bind with low affinity to both the isolated FERM and ezrin-CTD.
evidence: This claim is supported by binding data shown in Figure 3.

claim: PIP2 priming of ezrin loosens the association between the FERM and ezrin-CTD, allowing LOK-C to pry the domains apart, acting like a wedge, and thus permitting the kinase domain access to T567 in the ezrin-CTD.
source: Thus, PIP2 priming of ezrin loosens the association between the FERM and ezrin-CTD, allowing LOK-C to pry the domains apart, acting like a wedge, and thus permitting the kinase domain access to T567 in the ezrin-CTD.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data and represents the wedge model.

claim: Using a cross-linking approach ex vivo, LOK is recovered more efficiently with open ezrin rather than with closed ezrin-T567A that cannot be phosphorylated.
source: Indeed, using a cross-linking approach ex vivo, we have shown that LOK is recovered more efficiently with open ezrin rather than with closed ezrin-T567A that cannot be phosphorylated, suggesting that LOK has an affinity for sites masked in closed ezrin (Figure 6B, step 5) (Viswanatha et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: LOK has an affinity for sites masked in closed ezrin.
source: Indeed, using a cross-linking approach ex vivo, we have shown that LOK is recovered more efficiently with open ezrin rather than with closed ezrin-T567A that cannot be phosphorylated, suggesting that LOK has an affinity for sites masked in closed ezrin (Figure 6B, step 5) (Viswanatha et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is inferred from cross-linking data cited from prior work.

claim: LOK-C is a negative regulator of the kinase domain as it inhibits the activity of both LOK and LOK kinase domains toward ezrin or ezrin-CTD.
source: In this study we reveal that LOK-C is a negative regulator of the kinase domain as it inhibits the activity of both LOK and LOK kinase domains toward ezrin or ezrin-CTD.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Binding the ezrin-CTD likely relieves the inhibition of full-length LOK by LOK-C in cis.
source: Since LOK phosphorylates ezrin-CTD better than the isolated kinase domain does, binding the ezrin-CTD likely relieves the inhibition of full-length LOK by LOK-C in cis.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the kinetic and inhibition data.

claim: The C-terminal domain of SLK shares 56% sequence identity with LOK-C and undergoes homodimerization, a process that enhances kinase activity in vitro and ex vivo.
source: The C-terminal domain of SLK shares 56% sequence identity with LOK-C and undergoes homodimerization, a process that enhances kinase activity in vitro and ex vivo (Delarosa et al., 2011; Sabourin and Rudnicki, 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The specificity of kinases depends on local peptide consensus sequences, which in the case of ezrin phosphorylation by LOK involves the hydrophobic residue Y565 positioned -2 residues from T567.
source: The specificity of kinases depends on local peptide consensus sequences, which in the case of ezrin phosphorylation by LOK involves the hydrophobic residue Y565 positioned -2 residues from T567 (Belkina et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: A distal docking site within residues 520–530 in the ezrin-CTD is required for the efficient phosphorylation of T567 by either LOK or the isolated kinase domain.
source: As is seen with some other serine/threonine kinases (Biondi and Nebreda, 2003; Sharrocks et al., 2000; Ubersax and Ferrell, 2007), we have also identified a distal docking site within residues 520–530 in the ezrin-CTD, required for the efficient phosphorylation of T567 by either LOK or the isolated kinase domain (Figure 6B, steps 3–4), thereby adding another level of specificity to the kinase reaction.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Binding of the kinase to the distal docking site may relieve the inhibition imposed by LOK-C in the context of the full-length LOK.
source: Binding of the kinase to this site may also relieve the inhibition imposed by LOK-C in the context of the full-length LOK.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the experimental findings.

claim: The residues equivalent to ezrin 520–530 are relatively conserved, and Y565 and T567 perfectly conserved, in all ERM proteins.
source: It is interesting to note that the residues equivalent to ezrin 520–530 are relatively conserved, and Y565 and T567 perfectly conserved, in all ERM proteins, but not in the closely related merlin that also undergoes a similar FERM/merlin-CTD interaction, where the threonine equivalent to ezrin-T567 is not phosphorylated (Nguyen et al., 2001; Sher et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work and represents sequence analysis.

claim: In the closely related merlin, the threonine equivalent to ezrin-T567 is not phosphorylated.
source: It is interesting to note that the residues equivalent to ezrin 520–530 are relatively conserved, and Y565 and T567 perfectly conserved, in all ERM proteins, but not in the closely related merlin that also undergoes a similar FERM/merlin-CTD interaction, where the threonine equivalent to ezrin-T567 is not phosphorylated (Nguyen et al., 2001; Sher et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: At the genetic level, cells lacking LOK exhibit greatly reduced ezrin phosphorylation.
source: At the genetic level, cells lacking LOK exhibit greatly reduced ezrin phosphorylation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: On the subcellular level, LOK-C targets the kinase to the apical membrane.
source: On the subcellular level, LOK-C targets the kinase to the apical membrane (Viswanatha et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: LOK-mediated ezrin phosphorylation is the first example of a specific requirement for a phosphoinositide binding to the substrate for kinase activity.
source: While substrate specificity of protein kinases has been the subject of many studies (Ubersax and Ferrell, 2007), fewer cases of conditional specificity have been examined in detail, with LOK-mediated ezrin phosphorylation being the first example of a specific requirement for a phosphoinositide binding to the substrate.
evidence: This claim is based on the authors' knowledge of the field and the experimental findings.

claim: Complex cell behaviors rely on the proper timing of phosphorylation events.
source: As complex cell behaviors rely on the proper timing of phosphorylation events, such intimate co-regulation between substrates and kinases as described here may emerge as a general theme.
evidence: This is a general principle stated in the discussion.

claim: Intimate co-regulation between substrates and kinases as described for LOK and ezrin may emerge as a general theme.
source: As complex cell behaviors rely on the proper timing of phosphorylation events, such intimate co-regulation between substrates and kinases as described here may emerge as a general theme.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about broader implications.
